listLead: Hold'em is only the beginning. Every variant below is explained from scratch: its rules, how it differs from Hold'em, a hand played step by step and a short quiz. The ones marked "Playable" can be played right away against bots.

detail.walkthroughLead: Follow a full hand step by step. Use the arrows, the dots or your keyboard's ← → keys.
detail.quizLead: Five short questions. You get instant feedback after each answer.
detail.ctaPlayLead: Play a few hands against bots. The coach explains every decision.
detail.ctaSimilarLead: This variant cannot be played on the site yet, but a close relative can:

stepPlayer.privateNote: Dashed outline = private card (face down for the others)

quizUi.perfect: Perfect score. You really know this one.
quizUi.good: Nice work. Review the explanations for the ones you missed.
quizUi.low: Good start. Go through the rules once more and try again.

holdem.name: Texas Hold'em
holdem.tagline: The world's most popular poker game
holdem.summary: Each player gets two private cards and shares five community cards in the middle of the table. You make the best five-card hand from those seven cards. Easy to learn, hard to master: the perfect place to start.
rules: Each player is dealt 2 private cards face down. These are your hole cards.
Two forced bets start every hand: the small blind and the big blind. The two players to the left of the dealer button post them.
There are four betting rounds: preflop, flop, turn and river.
The flop puts 3 community cards face up in the middle. The turn adds a 4th card and the river a 5th.
Community cards belong to everyone. Your hand is the best 5 cards out of your 2 hole cards plus the 5 board cards. You can use both hole cards, one, or none.
On your turn you can check (pass without betting), bet, call (match a bet), raise (increase it) or fold (give up the hand).
In no-limit you can bet any amount, up to all of your chips (all-in), at any time.
If two or more players are still in after the river, there is a showdown: the best 5-card hand wins the pot.
The dealer button moves one seat clockwise after every hand, so everyone takes turns posting the blinds.
differences: This is the reference game: every other variant on this site is explained by comparing it to Hold'em.
Only 2 private cards, so hands are weaker on average than in Omaha. Top pair often wins.
No-limit betting: a single all-in can decide the hand at any moment.
There is no high/low split like in Hi-Lo; tied hands share the pot equally.
tips: Play fewer hands, but play them firmly. Most beginners call far too often.
Position matters: acting last (on the button) lets you see what others do first.
Always ask yourself: what is the best possible hand on this board right now?

steps.title: Blinds first
steps.text: Ada has the dealer button. Bora (small blind) puts in 1 chip and Cem (big blind) puts in 2. These forced bets make sure there is always something to play for.

steps.title: Two cards each
steps.text: Everyone gets 2 hole cards face down. Ada looks at hers: A♥ K♥. Two big cards of the same suit, a very strong start.

steps.title: Preflop betting
steps.text: Ada raises to 6. Bora folds and loses his 1-chip small blind. Cem calls 6. Two players go to the flop.

steps.title: The flop: K♦ 7♥ 2♥
steps.text: Three community cards appear. Ada now has top pair (kings) with the best kicker (ace). She also holds four hearts: one more heart gives her a flush.

steps.title: Flop betting
steps.text: Cem checks. Ada bets 8 to get value from her pair and build the pot. Cem calls. The pot is now 29.

steps.title: The turn: 9♠
steps.text: A blank card that changes nothing. Both players check, so the river comes for free.

steps.title: The river: 5♥
steps.text: The fifth heart! Ada's best 5 cards are A♥ K♥ 7♥ 5♥ 2♥, an ace-high flush. Nobody can have a better flush, so it is called the nut flush.

steps.title: River betting
steps.text: Cem bets 15. Ada raises to 40 because her hand is almost certainly the best. Cem calls.

steps.title: Showdown
steps.text: Cem shows Q♠ Q♦: a pair of queens. Ada's flush beats it easily. Notice that Ada used both hole cards and three board cards.

steps.title: Ada wins 109
steps.text: Ada collects the whole pot. The lesson: in Hold'em you always pick the best 5 cards out of the 7 available, and suited hands can turn into flushes.

quiz.q: How many hole cards does each player get in Texas Hold'em?
quiz.explain: Two private cards. The other five cards are shared on the board.

quiz.q: The board is K♦ 7♥ 2♥ 9♠ 5♥. Which hole cards make the best hand?
quiz.explain: K♣ K♠ plus the K♦ makes three kings, which beats three sevens. A♥ 3♣ only has four hearts, so no flush.

quiz.q: What is the river?
options: The fifth and last community card
quiz.explain: Flop = 3 cards, turn = 4th card, river = 5th card. The last betting round follows the river.

quiz.q: Who posts the big blind?
options: The player directly left of the dealer
The second player to the left of the dealer
The player who won the last hand
quiz.explain: Directly left of the button is the small blind; next to that is the big blind.

quiz.q: Do you have to use both of your hole cards?
options: No, any combination of 0, 1 or 2 hole cards is fine
Only when you have a pair
quiz.explain: In Hold'em you take the best 5 out of 7. If the board itself is the best hand, you can play the board. Omaha is the game where exactly two are required.

omaha.name: Omaha
omaha.tagline: Four cards, but you must use exactly two
omaha.summary: Omaha looks like Hold'em with four hole cards instead of two. The twist: your hand must use exactly two of your hole cards and exactly three board cards. Hands get much bigger, and that single rule catches out every beginner.
rules: Each player is dealt 4 hole cards face down.
The structure is the same as Hold'em: blinds, then preflop, flop, turn and river, with 5 community cards.
The golden rule: your final hand uses EXACTLY 2 of your hole cards and EXACTLY 3 board cards. Never more, never fewer.
So four hearts on the board plus one heart in your hand is NOT a flush. You need two hearts in your hand.
For example, with A-A-9 on the board and A-7 in your hand, you can use A and 7 with A-A-9 from the board to make three of a kind.
Omaha is usually played pot-limit: the most you can bet or raise is the size of the pot (counting your call first).
Straights, flushes and full houses are common, so a single pair rarely wins.
At showdown, each player shows the best legal 2 + 3 combination; the best hand wins.
differences: 4 hole cards instead of 2.
Exactly 2 hole cards + exactly 3 board cards. In Hold'em any combination is allowed.
Usually pot-limit instead of no-limit, so the maximum bet grows with the pot.
Winning hands are much stronger: top pair is often worth very little.
Many more draws are possible, so pots are often played by three or more players.
tips: Before every decision, physically count: two from my hand, three from the board.
Look for four cards that work together: two suited pairs or connected cards like K-Q-J-T.
Drawing to anything less than the best possible flush or straight is expensive in Omaha.

steps.title: Blinds
steps.text: Same start as Hold'em. Ada has the button, Bora posts 1, Cem posts 2. Everyone starts with 200 chips.

steps.title: Four cards each
steps.text: Ada gets A♠ K♥ Q♦ J♣. Four big cards look wonderful, but they are all different suits. Keep that in mind.

steps.title: Preflop
steps.text: Ada raises to 6. In pot-limit she could have raised to at most 7: after her call of 2 the pot would be 5, so she may raise by 5 more. Both opponents call. Pot: 18.

steps.title: Flop: K♠ 7♠ 2♠
steps.text: Three spades! Ada holds the A♠, so it is tempting to think she is drawing to the best flush. But she has only ONE spade, and Omaha needs two from the hand. She can never make a spade flush.

steps.title: Flop betting
steps.text: Ada bets 12 with her pair of kings (K♥ + K♠ on board). Bora and Cem both call. Pot: 54.

steps.title: Turn: T♠
steps.text: Now there are four spades and A-K-Q-J-T seems to be everywhere. Is it a straight? No: the board has only K and T, so Ada would need A, Q and J from her hand, which is three cards. No flush, no straight: still just a pair of kings.

steps.title: Ada folds
steps.text: Bora bets 40, Cem calls. Ada reads her hand correctly and folds. Many beginners would lose a big pot here.

steps.title: River: 4♥
steps.text: Bora bets 50 and Cem calls. Pot before the showdown: 234.

steps.title: Showdown
steps.text: Bora shows 9♠ 8♠: two spades in hand + K♠ T♠ 7♠ = king-high flush. Cem shows T♣ T♥: with the T♠ on board that is three tens. Both used exactly two hole cards.

steps.title: Bora wins 234
steps.text: The flush beats three of a kind. Ada saved her chips because she remembered the rule: exactly 2 from the hand, exactly 3 from the board.

quiz.q: How many of your hole cards must you use in Omaha?
quiz.explain: Always exactly 2 hole cards and exactly 3 board cards.

quiz.q: The board is A♥ K♥ 8♥ 4♥ 2♣ and you hold Q♥ J♠ T♠ 9♦. Do you have a flush?
options: No, you need two hearts in your hand
quiz.explain: With only one heart in your hand you can use at most one heart. Three board hearts + one hand heart = four hearts, not a flush.

quiz.q: The board is 7♣ 7♦ 7♥ K♠ 2♦. Which hand is best?
quiz.explain: 7♠ plus any second card, with 7♣ 7♦ 7♥ from the board, is four of a kind. Two hole cards + three board cards, perfectly legal. K-K only makes kings full of sevens.

quiz.q: In pot-limit, what is the largest raise you can make?
options: The size of the pot after you have called
quiz.explain: First imagine you call; the pot at that moment is the maximum you can raise on top.

quiz.q: The board is 9♠ 8♦ 3♣ 3♥ K♦ and you hold 3♠ A♣ A♦ Q♥. What is your best hand?
options: Full house, aces full of threes
quiz.explain: Use A♣ A♦ and 3♣ 3♥ K♦ from the board to make aces full of threes, using exactly 2 hole cards and 3 board cards.

omahaHiLo.name: Omaha Hi-Lo
omahaHiLo.tagline: Half the pot to the best high, half to the best low
omahaHiLo.summary: Omaha Hi-Lo (also called Omaha Eight-or-better) is played like Omaha, but the pot is usually split in two: the best high hand takes one half and the best qualifying low hand takes the other. A low only counts if it has five different cards of 8 or lower. Winning both halves is called scooping.
rules: Played like Omaha: 4 hole cards, 5 community cards, and you must use exactly 2 hole cards and 3 board cards. This applies to both the high and the low hand.
At showdown the pot is split: half to the best high hand, half to the best low hand.
A low hand must qualify with "8 or better": five cards of different ranks, all 8 or lower.
For the low the ace counts as 1 (the lowest card). Straights and flushes do not hurt a low hand.
The best possible low is A-2-3-4-5, called the wheel.
Lows are compared from the highest card down: 7-5-4-2-A beats 8-4-3-2-A because 7 is lower than 8.
A low is only possible if at least three different board cards are 8 or lower. If nobody has a qualifying low, the high hand wins the whole pot.
You may use different pairs of hole cards for your high and your low.
Winning both halves is a scoop. It is the real goal of the game. Usually played fixed-limit (pot-limit is also common).
differences: The pot can be split between a high hand and a low hand. In Hold'em one hand wins everything.
Low hands need the 8-or-better qualifier.
Exactly 2 hole cards + 3 board cards, as in Omaha, separately for high and low.
Hands with A-2 are the most valuable starting cards because they make the best lows.
Usually fixed-limit: bets come in fixed small and big sizes.
tips: Aim to scoop. Hands that can win only half the pot are expensive to play.
A-2 with a second suited ace or a few more low cards is a premium start.
Watch out for being quartered: if two players share the low, each gets only a quarter of the pot.

steps.title: Blinds and limits
steps.text: Fixed-limit game: bets are 2 on the preflop and flop, 4 on the turn and river. Bora posts 1, Cem posts 2.

steps.title: Four cards each
steps.text: Ada gets A♥ 2♦ 3♣ K♦. A-2 is the dream start for the low half: they are the two lowest cards.

steps.title: Preflop
steps.text: Ada raises to 4. Bora and Cem call. Pot: 12.

steps.title: Flop: K♣ 7♦ 4♠
steps.text: Only two board cards (7 and 4) are 8 or lower. A low needs three low board cards, so no low is possible yet. Ada also has a pair of kings for the high.

steps.title: Flop betting
steps.text: Bora bets 2. Cem gives up and folds. Ada calls: one more low card on the board gives her a strong low. Pot: 16.

steps.title: Turn: 5♥
steps.text: The third low card! Ada uses A♥ 2♦ with 7♦ 5♥ 4♠: her low is 7-5-4-2-A. Only a few hands can beat it.

steps.title: Turn betting
steps.text: Now the big bet (4) applies. Bora bets 4, Ada raises to 8, Bora calls. Pot: 32.

steps.title: River: Q♦
steps.text: Bora bets 4, Ada calls. Pot: 40.

steps.title: Showdown: two winners
steps.text: High: Bora's K♠ K♥ + K♣ Q♦ 7♦ is three kings, the best high hand. Low: Ada's 7-5-4-2-A. Bora has no cards of 8 or lower, so he cannot make a low at all.

steps.title: The pot is split
steps.text: Each takes 20. If Ada had also had the best high hand she would have taken all 40: that is a scoop.

quiz.q: What does "8 or better" mean?
options: The high hand must be at least a pair of eights
A low hand needs five different cards, all 8 or lower
You need an 8 in your hand
quiz.explain: To qualify for the low half, all five cards must be different ranks of 8 or below.

quiz.q: The board is 2♣ 5♦ 9♠ K♥ Q♣. Can anyone make a low?
options: No, only two board cards are 8 or lower
quiz.explain: You must use 3 board cards, and they all need to be 8 or lower. Here only 2 and 5 are.

quiz.q: Which low hand is best?
quiz.explain: Compare the highest card first: 6 is lower than 7 and 8. In ace-to-five low, the straight does not count against you.

quiz.q: What is a scoop?
options: Winning both the high and the low half
quiz.explain: Taking the whole pot by winning both halves (or winning high when no low qualifies).

quiz.q: The board is A♠ 4♦ 7♣ K♥ 9♠ and you hold 2♥ 3♥ Q♠ Q♦. What is your low?
quiz.explain: 2♥ 3♥ from your hand + A♠ 4♦ 7♣ from the board = 7-4-3-2-A, a qualifying low.

sevenCardStud.name: Seven Card Stud
sevenCardStud.tagline: No community cards: read what your opponents show
sevenCardStud.summary: The classic before Hold'em took over. Every player gets their own seven cards: three face down and four face up. There is no board; instead you watch the face-up cards of your opponents and guess what they are hiding.
rules: There are no community cards. Each player receives 7 cards of their own: 3 face down and 4 face up.
Everyone puts in an ante (a small forced bet) before the deal. There are no blinds.
3rd street: two cards face down and one card face up for each player.
The player with the lowest face-up card must post the bring-in, a small forced bet. If two upcards tie, suit decides (clubs lowest, then diamonds, hearts, spades).
4th, 5th and 6th street: one more face-up card each, followed by a betting round.
7th street (the river) is dealt face down.
From 4th street on, the player with the best visible hand acts first.
Fixed-limit: the small bet is used on 3rd and 4th street, the big bet on 5th, 6th and 7th.
At showdown you pick your best 5 cards out of 7.
differences: No shared board: all 7 cards belong to you.
Some of your cards are visible to everyone, so you can read opponents (and they can read you).
Antes and a bring-in instead of small and big blinds; no fixed dealer-button order.
The acting order changes every street depending on who shows the best cards.
Folded upcards are dead cards: remembering them tells you which cards are gone.
tips: Remember folded cards: if three of your flush cards were folded, your draw is much weaker.
Hidden pairs (like aces in the hole) are strong because nobody can see them.
Big pairs showing on board represent strength: be careful against them.

steps.title: Antes
steps.text: Everyone puts in 1 chip as an ante. Pot: 3. Stud has no blinds and no community cards.

steps.title: 3rd street
steps.text: Each player gets two cards face down and one face up. Ada sees her hidden A♥ A♦ (the dashed outline means the others cannot see them) and shows 9♣. Bora shows 2♦, Cem T♥.

steps.title: Bring-in
steps.text: The lowest upcard posts the bring-in. That is Bora's 2♦, so he puts in 2 chips.

steps.title: Completing the bet
steps.text: Cem completes to 4 (a full small bet). Ada just calls to hide her strength. Bora calls too. Pot: 15.

steps.title: 4th street
steps.text: New upcards: Ada K♦, Bora 5♥, Cem 7♦. Ada's K-9 is the best visible hand, so she acts first: she bets 4. Bora folds, Cem calls.

steps.title: 5th street
steps.text: Ada gets 9♥ (she now has aces and nines), Cem gets T♣. Cem's pair of tens showing beats Ada's visible nines, so he acts first and bets 8, the big bet. Ada calls.

steps.title: 6th street
steps.text: Ada 2♠, Cem 3♦. Nothing changes. Both check.

steps.title: 7th street
steps.text: The last card comes face down: Ada 3♣, Cem Q♥. Cem bets 8, Ada calls. Pot: 55.

steps.title: Showdown
steps.text: Cem turns over K♠ K♣: two pair, kings and tens. Ada shows aces and nines. Two pair against two pair: the higher top pair wins, and aces beat kings.

steps.title: Ada wins 55
steps.text: Her aces stayed hidden the whole time. In Stud, think about what can be hidden behind the cards you see.

quiz.q: How many cards does each player get in Seven Card Stud (if they play to the end)?
quiz.explain: Seven: 3 face down (2 at the start and the last one) and 4 face up.

quiz.q: Who posts the bring-in on 3rd street?
options: The player left of the dealer
quiz.explain: The player with the lowest upcard is forced to start the betting (in Razz it is the reverse: the highest upcard).

quiz.q: How many of your 7 cards are face down?
quiz.explain: The first two cards and the 7th street card are face down.

quiz.q: Who acts first from 4th street on?
options: The player with the best visible hand
The player with the most chips
quiz.explain: Whoever shows the strongest face-up cards acts first on that street.

quiz.q: Which 7-card holding makes the best 5-card hand?
quiz.explain: 5-6-7-8-9 is a straight, which beats three queens and two pair. The last hand has only four clubs, so no flush.

razz.name: Razz
razz.tagline: Stud where the lowest hand wins
razz.summary: Razz is Seven Card Stud turned upside down: the lowest hand wins the whole pot. Aces are low, and straights and flushes do not count, so the best possible hand is 5-4-3-2-A. Pairs are what you fear.
rules: Dealt exactly like Seven Card Stud: antes, 2 cards down + 1 up, then 4th to 6th street face up and 7th street face down.
The LOWEST 5-card hand wins the whole pot. There is no qualifier: some low always wins.
The ace is always low (it counts as 1).
Straights and flushes are ignored. 5-4-3-2-A (the wheel) is the best possible hand.
Pairs are bad: you want five different ranks. A hand with a pair loses to any hand without one.
Compare from the highest card down: 7-6-5-4-3 beats 8-4-3-2-A because 7 is lower than 8.
The bring-in is posted by the HIGHEST upcard (a king is the worst card).
From 4th street on, the LOWEST visible hand acts first.
Usually fixed-limit.
differences: The lowest hand wins, not the highest.
Ace is low; straights and flushes do not exist for ranking.
No community cards: it is a stud game.
Bring-in and acting order are reversed compared with Seven Card Stud.
Pairs, which are good in Hold'em, ruin your hand here.
tips: Start with three different cards of 8 or lower; anything else is usually a fold.
A high face-up card like a king (a brick) hurts you, and everyone can see it.
Watch the low cards others show: they are cards you can no longer receive.

steps.title: Antes
steps.text: Everyone antes 1. Pot: 3. The dealing is the same as Seven Card Stud.

steps.title: 3rd street
steps.text: Ada has A♠ 3♦ hidden and shows 5♣: three perfect low cards. Bora shows Q♠, Cem 6♠.

steps.title: Bring-in: the highest card
steps.text: In Razz the HIGHEST upcard pays the bring-in, the opposite of Stud. Bora's Q♠ is the worst card on the table, so he posts 2.

steps.title: Completing
steps.text: Cem completes to 4, Ada calls and Bora folds. Pot: 13.

steps.title: 4th street
steps.text: Ada gets 2♥: A-2-3-5, four low cards. Cem gets 3♠. Ada's 5-2 showing is the lowest, so she acts first: she bets 4, Cem calls.

steps.title: 5th street
steps.text: Ada gets K♣, a brick. Cem gets 8♣. Cem's 8-6-3 now looks better than Ada's K-5-2, so he acts first and bets 8. Ada calls: she still has four great low cards.

steps.title: 6th street
steps.text: Ada catches 7♠ and has a made hand: 7-5-3-2-A. Cem gets 8♥, pairing his eight, which is bad in Razz. Ada's board is lower now, so she bets 8 and Cem calls.

steps.title: 7th street
steps.text: Face-down cards: Ada 8♦, Cem T♦. Ada bets 8, Cem calls. Pot: 69.

steps.title: Showdown
steps.text: Cem's best is 8-6-4-3-2. Ada's is 7-5-3-2-A. Compare the highest cards: 7 is lower than 8, so Ada wins all 69. Cem's two spades do not matter at all.

quiz.q: What is the best possible hand in Razz?
quiz.explain: The ace is low and straights do not count, so A-2-3-4-5 is the perfect low.

quiz.q: Which hand wins in Razz?
quiz.explain: Compare the highest card: 7 is the lowest top card. That it is a straight is irrelevant.

quiz.q: Who posts the bring-in in Razz?
quiz.explain: The worst Razz card showing (highest) pays the bring-in.

quiz.q: Does a flush hurt your hand in Razz?
options: Yes, it counts as a flush
Only if it is a heart flush
quiz.explain: Razz uses ace-to-five low: straights and flushes are ignored.

quiz.q: Which of these lows is best?
quiz.explain: 6-5-4-2-A vs 6-5-4-3-2: tied on 6, 5 and 4, then 2 beats 3. The flush is ignored; the pair of fives is worst.

fiveCardDraw.name: Five Card Draw
fiveCardDraw.summary: The simplest poker there is: five private cards, one chance to swap some of them, and two betting rounds. No community cards and no face-up cards: the only clue about an opponent's hand is how many cards they draw.
rules: Each player is dealt 5 private cards face down. There are no community cards.
Blinds (or antes) start the pot.
First betting round: starting left of the big blind.
The draw: in turn, each player discards 0 to 5 cards and receives the same number of new ones. Keeping all five is called standing pat.
Second betting round: starting with the first active player left of the dealer.
Showdown: the best 5-card poker hand wins.
Usually fixed-limit: the bet size doubles after the draw.
How many cards an opponent draws is your best information about their hand.
differences: No community cards: every card is yours and private.
A draw round replaces flop, turn and river.
Only two betting rounds.
Your only read on opponents is how many cards they change and how they bet.
tips: With a pair, keep the pair and draw three. Keeping a kicker usually lowers your chances.
Drawing one card often means two pair or a straight/flush draw; drawing three usually means one pair.
Do not chase a straight draw open at only one end (inside straight): it hits rarely.

steps.title: Blinds
steps.text: Ada has the button. Bora posts the small blind (1), Cem the big blind (2). Fixed-limit: bets are 2 before the draw and 4 after.

steps.title: Five cards each
steps.text: Ada gets J♠ J♦ 8♣ 4♥ 2♠: a pair of jacks, a solid start.

steps.title: First betting round
steps.text: Ada raises to 4. Bora and Cem both call. Pot: 12.

steps.title: Planning the draw
steps.text: Ada keeps her pair of jacks. The 8♣ 4♥ 2♠ do not help, so she will throw all three away.

steps.title: Discards
steps.text: Bora throws 1 card, Cem 2, Ada 3. Useful information: Bora's single card suggests a flush or straight draw, Cem's two suggests three of a kind.

steps.title: New cards
steps.text: Ada receives J♥ 9♦ 3♣: three jacks! Her opponents' new cards stay hidden.

steps.title: Second betting round
steps.text: Bora checks. Cem bets 4. Ada raises to 8. Bora missed his flush and folds. Cem calls. Pot: 28.

steps.title: Showdown
steps.text: Cem shows 6♣ 6♦ 6♥: three sixes. Ada's three jacks are higher.

steps.title: Ada wins 28
steps.text: By drawing three to her pair she gave herself the best chance to improve, and it worked.

quiz.q: How many cards do you get in Five Card Draw?
quiz.explain: Five private cards, no community cards.

quiz.q: What does standing pat mean?
options: Keeping all five cards and drawing none
quiz.explain: A pat player is happy with the hand, often a straight, flush or better.

quiz.q: You hold 9♠ 9♦ K♣ 6♥ 2♣. What is the usual play?
quiz.explain: Keeping only the pair and drawing three gives the most chances to make three of a kind or two pair.

quiz.q: After the draw, which hand wins?
quiz.explain: Three eights beat two pair, one pair and ace high (the third hand is not a flush: the 9♦ is a different suit).

quiz.q: An opponent draws exactly one card. What does this most often mean?
options: Two pair or a four-card straight/flush draw
quiz.explain: One card is drawn with two pair or with a draw to a straight or flush.

deuceToSevenTripleDraw.name: 2-7 Triple Draw
deuceToSevenTripleDraw.tagline: Lowball with three draws, and the ace is high
deuceToSevenTripleDraw.summary: In Deuce-to-Seven (2-7) the worst traditional poker hand wins. Aces are high, and straights and flushes count against you, so the best hand is 7-5-4-3-2 in mixed suits. You get three draws to build it.
rules: Lowball: the lowest hand wins the pot.
The ace is ALWAYS high. A-2-3-4-5 is not a straight here, but an ace-high hand, which is bad.
Straights and flushes count against you: 7-6-5-4-3 is a straight and loses to almost everything.
The best possible hand: 7-5-4-3-2 of at least two suits, called "number one".
Any unpaired hand without a straight or flush beats every paired hand.
Each player gets 5 cards. There are three draws and four betting rounds.
Blinds start the pot. Fixed-limit: small bet in the first two rounds, big bet in the last two.
Compare from the highest card down: 8-6-5-4-3 beats 8-7-4-3-2 because 6 is lower than 7.
Standing pat (not drawing) usually means a made hand.
differences: The lowest hand wins instead of the highest.
Ace is high only; straights and flushes ruin your hand.
No community cards; three draws instead of flop, turn and river.
Four betting rounds with fixed small and big bets.
Different from Razz: in Razz the ace is low and straights/flushes do not count.
tips: A 2 is the most important card: without it you can never have the best hands.
Start with three or more different cards of 7 or lower, including the 2.
When an opponent stands pat early, you need to improve quickly.

steps.title: Blinds
steps.text: Bora posts 1, Cem posts 2. Bets are 2 in the first two rounds and 4 in the last two.

steps.title: Five cards each
steps.text: Ada holds 2♦ 4♣ 7♥ K♦ K♠. 2-4-7 is a great start for a low; the pair of kings is useless.

steps.title: First betting round
steps.text: Ada raises to 4. Bora folds. Cem calls. Pot: 9.

steps.title: First draw
steps.text: Cem draws 1, Ada draws 2 (both kings). Ada receives 3♠ and A♣. Careful: the ace is HIGH in 2-7, so A-7-4-3-2 is only an ace-high hand.

steps.title: Second betting round
steps.text: Cem bets 2, Ada calls. Pot: 13.

steps.title: Second draw
steps.text: Cem stands pat: he is happy with his five cards. Ada throws the A♣ and gets 9♥: 9-7-4-3-2.

steps.title: Third betting round
steps.text: Now the big bet: Cem bets 4, Ada calls. Pot: 21.

steps.title: Third draw
steps.text: Cem stands pat again. Ada throws the 9♥ and catches 6♣: 7-6-4-3-2. No pair, no straight (the 5 is missing), no flush. A very strong hand.

steps.title: Last betting round
steps.text: Cem bets 4, Ada raises to 8, Cem calls. Pot: 37.

steps.title: Showdown
steps.text: Cem shows 8-6-5-4-3. Ada has 7-6-4-3-2. The top card decides: 7 beats 8, so Ada wins 37.

quiz.q: What is the best possible hand in 2-7 lowball?
quiz.explain: A-2-3-4-5 is ace high, 2-3-4-5-6 is a straight and the all-hearts version is a flush.

quiz.q: How does the ace count in 2-7?
options: It is removed from the deck
quiz.explain: In deuce-to-seven the ace is always the highest card, which makes it bad for a low hand.

quiz.q: Which hand wins in 2-7?
quiz.explain: 7-6-5-4-3 is a straight, A-5-4-3-2 is ace high and the last one is a flush. The 8-6 is the best low.

quiz.q: How many draws are there in Triple Draw?
quiz.explain: Three draws, with a betting round before each draw and one after the last.

quiz.q: Which is lower (better): 8-6-5-4-3 or 8-7-4-3-2?
quiz.explain: Both start with 8; the next card decides, and 6 is lower than 7.

shortDeck.name: Short Deck Hold'em
shortDeck.tagline: Hold'em with a 36-card deck: a flush beats a full house
shortDeck.summary: Short Deck (also called 6+ Hold'em) is played like Hold'em, but all 2s, 3s, 4s and 5s are removed. With fewer cards, the hand rankings change: a flush becomes rarer than a full house, so it ranks higher. The action is wild and draws hit often.
rules: Played like Hold'em: 2 hole cards, flop, turn, river and 4 betting rounds.
The deck has 36 cards: 6 through ace in each suit. Cards 2 to 5 are removed.
The ace can also play low in the straight A-6-7-8-9 (the lowest straight).
A flush beats a full house, because with only nine cards per suit flushes are rarer.
In most modern rules three of a kind also beats a straight. Some games keep straight above trips, so check the table's rules.
Usually everyone pays an ante instead of blinds (often with an extra button blind).
Usually played no-limit.
Best 5 cards out of 7 wins, as in Hold'em.
differences: 36-card deck: no 2, 3, 4 or 5.
A flush beats a full house.
A-6-7-8-9 is a straight (the ace plays low).
Antes instead of blinds in most games.
Hands run closer: draws come in much more often than in Hold'em.
tips: Before playing, check the ranking used at your table: does trips beat a straight?
Flush draws are weaker than you think: there are fewer cards of each suit left.
Big pairs lose value; connected cards gain value.

walkthrough.title: When a flush beats a full house

steps.title: Antes
steps.text: Everyone antes 1. Pot: 3. The deck has only 36 cards: 6 through ace.

steps.title: Two cards each
steps.text: Ada: A♥ 9♣. Bora: K♦ K♣. Cem: J♠ T♠.

steps.title: Preflop
steps.text: Bora raises to 6. Cem and Ada call. Pot: 21.

steps.title: Flop: 6♥ 7♦ 8♠
steps.text: Ada has a straight already: A-6-7-8-9, with the ace playing low. That straight only exists in Short Deck. She bets 10 and both opponents call. Pot: 51.

steps.title: Turn: K♠
steps.text: Bora now has three kings. Cem has four spades and needs one more for a flush. Bora bets 20 and everyone calls. Pot: 111.

steps.title: River: 7♠
steps.text: Bora makes a full house (kings full of sevens), Cem makes a flush. Bora bets 30, Cem moves all-in for 63, Ada folds her straight and Bora calls.

steps.title: Bora's full house
steps.text: Bora shows K♦ K♣ for K-K-K-7-7. In regular Hold'em this would beat a flush and win the pot.

steps.title: Cem's flush is higher
steps.text: Cem shows J♠ T♠ with K♠ 8♠ 7♠ for a flush. In Short Deck the flush outranks the full house.

steps.title: Cem wins 237
steps.text: Same cards, different rules, different winner. Always remember: in Short Deck, flush beats full house.

quiz.q: Which cards are removed in Short Deck?
quiz.explain: 2s, 3s, 4s and 5s are removed: 36 cards remain.

quiz.q: In Short Deck, which is higher?
quiz.explain: With nine cards per suit a flush is rarer than a full house, so it ranks higher.

quiz.q: Is A-6-7-8-9 a straight in Short Deck?
quiz.explain: With 2-5 gone, the ace connects to the 6 to form the lowest straight.

quiz.q: The board is 9♥ 8♥ 7♣ K♥ 6♦. Which hand wins in Short Deck?
quiz.explain: A♥ J♥ with 9♥ 8♥ K♥ makes a flush. T-J makes a jack-high straight and K-K or 9-9 make three of a kind; the flush beats them all.

quiz.q: What do players usually pay instead of blinds in Short Deck?
quiz.explain: Most Short Deck games use antes from everyone, often plus a button blind.

pineapple.name: Pineapple
pineapple.tagline: Hold'em with one extra card to throw away
pineapple.summary: Pineapple is Hold'em with a twist: you get three hole cards and must discard one of them. In standard Pineapple you discard before the flop; in Crazy Pineapple you keep all three until the flop betting is over. After that, it plays exactly like Hold'em.
rules: Each player is dealt 3 hole cards instead of 2.
Standard Pineapple: you discard one of the three before the flop (usually right after the preflop betting round).
Crazy Pineapple: you keep all three through the flop and discard after the flop betting round.
After the discard you have 2 hole cards and play exactly like Hold'em: any combination of your 2 cards and the 5 board cards.
Discarded cards are face down and out of play (dead).
Blinds and four betting rounds as in Hold'em; usually no-limit.
The best 5-card hand wins at showdown.
differences: 3 hole cards instead of 2, with one discard.
The discard timing depends on the version (before the flop, or after the flop betting in Crazy Pineapple).
Starting hands are stronger on average, so winning hands are too.
After the discard, every Hold'em rule applies unchanged.
tips: Keep the two cards that work best together: pairs, suited cards, connected cards.
Expect opponents to hold better hands than in Hold'em.
In Crazy Pineapple, use the flop to decide which card to keep.

steps.title: Blinds
steps.text: Ada is on the button. Bora posts 1, Cem posts 2.

steps.title: Three cards each
steps.text: Ada gets A♥ Q♥ 7♣. She already knows which card she will throw away.

steps.title: Preflop
steps.text: Ada raises to 6. Bora calls. Cem folds and loses his big blind. Pot: 14.

steps.title: The discard
steps.text: Ada discards the 7♣ and keeps the suited A♥ Q♥. Bora discards one card face down and keeps 9♠ 9♦. From now on it is plain Hold'em.

steps.title: Flop: Q♦ T♥ 3♥
steps.text: Ada has top pair (queens) and a draw to the best flush. She bets 8 and Bora calls. Pot: 30.

steps.title: Turn: 2♣
steps.text: Nothing changes. Both check.

steps.title: River: 8♥
steps.text: The flush arrives: A♥ Q♥ T♥ 8♥ 3♥. Ada bets 20, Bora calls. Pot: 70.

steps.title: Showdown
steps.text: Bora shows 9♠ 9♦, a pair of nines. Ada's ace-high flush wins.

steps.title: Ada wins 70
steps.text: Had she kept the 7♣ instead of the Q♥, she would have no flush at all. In Pineapple the discard is your first important decision.

quiz.q: How many hole cards do you start with in Pineapple?
quiz.explain: Three, and you must discard one.

quiz.q: When do you discard in Crazy Pineapple?
quiz.explain: In Crazy Pineapple you see the flop with three cards and discard after the flop betting.

quiz.q: You hold K♠ K♦ 4♣. Which card do you discard?
quiz.explain: Keep the pair of kings.

quiz.q: After the discard, how is the game played?
quiz.explain: With 2 hole cards the rest is identical to Texas Hold'em.

quiz.q: The board is Q♦ T♥ 3♥ 2♣ 8♥. Which two kept cards win?
quiz.explain: A♥ Q♥ makes an ace-high flush. J-9 makes a queen-high straight (Q-J-T-9-8), which the flush beats.

badugi.name: Badugi
badugi.tagline: Four cards, four suits, as low as possible
badugi.summary: Badugi is a lowball draw game with four cards. You want four cards of different suits and different ranks, as low as possible. Such a hand is called a badugi. Aces are low, and the best hand is A-2-3-4 in four different suits.
rules: Each player gets 4 private cards. There are three draws and four betting rounds, like Triple Draw.
Blinds start the pot. Usually fixed-limit: small bets in the first two rounds, big bets in the last two.
The goal: the lowest hand made of cards with all different suits AND all different ranks.
Four valid cards is a badugi. The ace is low, so A-2-3-4 of four suits is the best possible hand.
If two cards share a suit or a rank, only one of them counts: you have a 3-card hand (or 2 or 1 card).
Any 4-card badugi beats any 3-card hand, and any 3-card hand beats any 2-card hand.
Hands with the same number of cards are compared from the highest card down: 8-6-4-2 beats 9-3-2-A.
Straights do not matter.
Standing pat usually shows a made badugi.
differences: 4 cards instead of 2, and no community cards.
The lowest hand wins, judged by suits and ranks, not by poker hand rankings.
Three draws and four betting rounds.
Suits matter in a new way: duplicate suits make your hand smaller.
tips: A 3-card hand with very low cards (like A-2-3) is a good drawing hand.
A high badugi (with a Q or K) can be worth breaking to draw for a better one, early on.
Count how many cards opponents draw: a pat player usually has a badugi.

steps.title: Blinds
steps.text: Bora posts 1, Cem posts 2. Fixed-limit: 2 in the first two rounds, 4 in the last two.

steps.title: Four cards each
steps.text: Ada has A♠ 3♦ 5♥ K♥. The 5♥ and K♥ share a suit, so only A-3-5 counts: a 3-card hand.

steps.title: First betting round
steps.text: Ada raises to 4. Bora folds. Cem calls with Q♠ 6♦ 4♣ 2♥, a badugi but a high one. Pot: 9.

steps.title: First draw
steps.text: Ada throws the K♥ and gets 8♥: another heart, still only 3 cards. Cem breaks his queen badugi, draws 1 and gets 9♣ (clubs twice): also a 3-card hand now.

steps.title: Second betting round
steps.text: Cem checks, Ada bets 2, Cem calls. Pot: 13.

steps.title: Second draw
steps.text: Ada throws the 8♥ and gets 2♣: A♠ 2♣ 3♦ 5♥, four suits, four ranks. A badugi! Cem throws the 9♣ and gets 8♠: 8-6-4-2, also a badugi.

steps.title: Third betting round
steps.text: Big bets now. Cem bets 4, Ada raises to 8, Cem calls. Pot: 29.

steps.title: Third draw
steps.text: Both players stand pat.

steps.title: Last betting round
steps.text: Cem checks, Ada bets 4, Cem calls. Pot: 37.

steps.title: Showdown
steps.text: Both have a 4-card badugi, so compare the highest card: Ada's 5-3-2-A against Cem's 8-6-4-2. 5 is lower, so Ada wins 37.

quiz.q: What is a badugi?
options: Four cards of the same suit
Four cards of different suits and different ranks
A pair plus two low cards
quiz.explain: All four suits and all four ranks must be different.

quiz.q: What is the best possible Badugi hand?
quiz.explain: The ace is low; A-2-3-4 with four different suits is unbeatable.

quiz.q: Which hand wins?
quiz.explain: K-Q-J-T in four suits is a real 4-card badugi. A♥ 2♥ 3♣ 4♦ has two hearts, so it is only a 3-card hand; the pair of fives also makes a 3-card hand. Any 4-card badugi beats any 3-card hand.

quiz.q: You hold 2♠ 4♦ 7♥ 7♣. How many cards count?
quiz.explain: The two sevens share a rank, so only one of them counts: 2-4-7 is a 3-card hand.

quiz.q: Which 4-card badugi is lower (better): 8-6-4-2 or 9-3-2-A?
quiz.explain: Compare the highest card: 8 is lower than 9.

horse.name: H.O.R.S.E.
horse.tagline: Five games in rotation: the all-rounder's test
horse.summary: HORSE is not a single game but a rotation of five: Hold'em, Omaha Hi-Lo, Razz, Seven Card Stud and Stud Eight-or-better. The game changes at regular intervals, so you need to be good at all of them. Everything is played fixed-limit.
rules: H = Limit Hold'em, O = Omaha Hi-Lo (8 or better), R = Razz, S = Seven Card Stud, E = Seven Card Stud Eight-or-better (Stud Hi-Lo).
The games are always played in the order H-O-R-S-E, then back to H.
The game changes after a fixed period: commonly one full orbit of the dealer button, or after a time level in tournaments.
All five games are fixed-limit, with a small bet and a big bet.
Hold'em and Omaha use blinds and a dealer button; the three stud games use antes and a bring-in.
Stud Eight-or-better is Seven Card Stud with a split pot: half to the best high, half to the best qualifying low (five different cards 8 or lower).
Your chips and seat stay the same; only the game changes.
It rewards all-round skill: a weakness in one game cannot be hidden for long.
differences: Not one game but five, played in turn.
Fixed-limit betting in every game, including Hold'em.
Includes high games (H, S), low games (R) and split games (O, E).
You must switch thinking each time: in Razz the lowest hand wins, in Stud the highest.
tips: Learn each game on its own first. On this site, Hold'em and Seven Card Stud are playable.
Before every hand, ask: which game is it now, and does the high or the low win?
Most mistakes happen right after the switch, so slow down for the first hands of each game.

steps.title: The rotation
steps.text: Same table, same players, same chips. Only the game changes: H → O → R → S → E, then back to H.

steps.title: H: Limit Hold'em
steps.text: Blinds, 2 hole cards and a board, exactly like Hold'em, but every bet is a fixed size. Ada has top pair: J♠ with the J♥ on board.

steps.title: O: Omaha Hi-Lo
steps.text: Four hole cards, exactly 2 + 3, and a split pot. Ada's A♥ 2♦ with 7-5-4 on board is a strong low.

steps.title: R: Razz
steps.text: Now the stud games begin: antes, bring-in and no board. In Razz the lowest hand wins: Ada's A-3-5-2 is excellent.

steps.title: S: Seven Card Stud
steps.text: Back to the highest hand. Ada's hidden aces plus a pair of nines showing make two pair.

steps.title: E: Stud Eight-or-better
steps.text: Stud with a split pot. Ada has A-2-3-4-5: the best low (and even a straight for high). Bora's queens full of jacks wins the high half. They split the pot.

steps.title: Back to the start
steps.text: After E the rotation starts again with Hold'em. The dealer button has moved on.

steps.title: H again
steps.text: Ada looks down at Q♥ Q♣ in Hold'em: a high hand, so higher is better again. Always ask: which game is it now?

quiz.q: What does the O stand for in HORSE?
quiz.explain: O is Omaha Eight-or-better, the split-pot version.

quiz.q: In what order are the games played?
quiz.explain: The order is fixed: Hold'em, Omaha Hi-Lo, Razz, Stud, Stud Eight-or-better.

quiz.q: What betting structure is used in HORSE?
quiz.explain: All five games are fixed-limit.

quiz.q: In which HORSE game does the lowest hand win the whole pot?
quiz.explain: Razz is the pure low game. O and E are split between high and low.

quiz.q: Which games use a split pot?
quiz.explain: Omaha Hi-Lo and Stud Eight-or-better split the pot between high and low.
